name: Northwest Ordinance (reenacted 1789)
citation: Act of Aug. 7, 1789, 1 Stat. 50 (reenacting the Ordinance of 1787)
summary: Article III promised that Indians' lands and property 'shall never be taken from them without their consent' and that 'utmost good faith' would be observed, language later invoked as a moral and legal benchmark; in practice followed by cessions.

name: Trade and Intercourse (Nonintercourse) Acts, 1790-1802
summary: Barred purchases of Indian land except by treaty or convention under federal authority and regulated trade and licensing; the 1790 Act is the root of the Nonintercourse Act relied on in Oneida II and Passamaquoddy.

name: Civilization Fund Act
summary: Authorized annual federal funds for missionary and other societies to run schools and teach agriculture, formalizing assimilation policy and the roots of Indian boarding-school policy.

name: Indian Removal Act
summary: Authorized the President to negotiate exchanges of eastern tribal land for land west of the Mississippi; used to remove the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Choctaw and Chickasaw. Removal treaties include Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) and New Echota (1835).

name: Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834
citation: Act of June 30, 1834, ch. 161, 4 Stat. 729 (section 12 at 4 Stat. 730 codified at 25 U.S.C. 177)
summary: Restated that no purchase, grant, lease or conveyance of Indian lands is valid unless made by treaty or convention under the Constitution; defined Indian country and federal criminal jurisdiction; source of 25 U.S.C. 177.

name: Indian Appropriations Act of 1851
summary: Appropriated funds for the Indian Department and treaty obligations, reorganized superintendencies and agencies, provided that treaties be negotiated by officers the President designates, and extended the trade and intercourse laws over the tribes of New Mexico and Utah.

name: Act of March 3, 1871 (end of treaty-making)
citation: Act of Mar. 3, 1871, ch. 120, 16 Stat. 544, 566; codified at 25 U.S.C. 71
summary: Provided that no tribe 'shall be acknowledged or recognized as an independent nation, tribe, or power with whom the United States may contract by treaty', while preserving treaties ratified before March 3, 1871. Replaced treaties with 'agreements' ratified by both houses.

name: Major Crimes Act
citation: Act of Mar. 3, 1885, ch. 341, 23 Stat. 362 (section 9, 23 Stat. 385), now 18 U.S.C. 1153
summary: Extended federal jurisdiction over enumerated serious crimes by Indians against anyone in Indian country, responding to Ex parte Crow Dog; upheld in Kagama (1886) and central to McGirt (2020).

name: General Allotment (Dawes) Act
citation: Act of Feb. 8, 1887, ch. 119, 24 Stat. 388 (25 U.S.C. 331 et seq., repealed by Pub. L. 106-462, title I, sec. 106(a)(1), Nov. 7, 2000, 114 Stat. 2007)
summary: Authorized division of reservations into individual allotments and sale of 'surplus' land to non-Indians. Secondary sources cite a drop in Native-held land from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million acres (1934); other estimates of land lost range around 90-100 million acres [figures vary by source].

name: Curtis Act
summary: Extended allotment to the Five Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole) in Indian Territory, abolished tribal courts, barred federal courts from enforcing tribal laws, and gave the Dawes Commission authority over enrollment; paved the way to Oklahoma statehood (1907).

name: Antiquities Act of 1906
summary: Authorizes the President to proclaim national monuments on federal land; used to protect tribal cultural landscapes (e.g., Bears Ears, 2016). Whether the President may shrink monuments is contested.

name: Burke Act
citation: Act of May 8, 1906, ch. 2348, 34 Stat. 182 (amending sec. 6 of the Dawes Act)
summary: Amended the Dawes Act to let the Secretary of the Interior end trust status early ('forced fee patents') for allottees deemed competent, which the Library of Congress calls the "Forced Fee Patenting Act."

name: Indian Citizenship Act
summary: Declared non-citizen Indians born in the U.S. to be citizens, without requiring them to renounce tribal membership and without impairing tribal property rights; state voting barriers continued for years.

name: Pueblo Lands Act
summary: Created the Pueblo Lands Board to adjudicate non-Indian claims on Pueblo lands in New Mexico, resolving title questions after United States v. Sandoval (1913).

name: Indian Reorganization Act (Wheeler-Howard Act)
citation: Act of June 18, 1934, 48 Stat. 984 (Pub. L. 73-383), 25 U.S.C. 5101 et seq. (section 5 at 25 U.S.C. 5108, formerly 465)
summary: Ended allotment; authorized the Secretary to take land into trust for tribes and individuals (section 5) and encouraged tribal constitutions (section 16). Secondary sources report over two million acres restored in the first two decades. Limited by Carcieri (2009) to tribes under federal jurisdiction in 1934.

name: Flood Control Act of 1944 (Pick-Sloan Plan)
summary: Authorized Missouri River dams (e.g., Garrison, Oahe, Fort Randall) whose reservoirs flooded fertile reservation bottomlands of the Three Affiliated Tribes, Standing Rock, Cheyenne River and others; compensation came later by separate acts. [Dam/tribe examples from-memory]

name: Indian Claims Commission Act
citation: Act of Aug. 13, 1946, ch. 959, 60 Stat. 1049; Commission terminated by Pub. L. 94-465 (1978)
summary: Created a forum for tribal claims against the United States but could award only money, not land return; secondary sources report 546 dockets completed and about $818 million in judgments, and some settlements were tied to termination.

name: House Concurrent Resolution 108 (termination policy)
citation: H. Con. Res. 108, 83d Cong., 1st Sess., 67 Stat. B132 (Aug. 1, 1953)
summary: Declared congressional policy to end federal supervision of tribes 'as rapidly as possible', launching the Termination Era (the National Archives says Congress initiated 60 termination proceedings from 1953 to 1970, and over three million acres of tribal land were relinquished).

name: Public Law 280
summary: Gave California, Minnesota (except Red Lake), Nebraska, Oregon (except Warm Springs), Wisconsin (except Menominee) and later Alaska criminal and civil adjudicatory jurisdiction over Indian country; the 1968 ICRA required tribal consent for future assumption and allowed retrocession.

name: Klamath Termination Act
summary: Terminated federal supervision of the Klamath Tribes; most of the reservation forest was sold or became national forest (the Wikipedia article reports a reservation reduction from 762,000 to 145,000 acres [secondary]); treaty hunting and fishing rights survived (Kimball v. Callahan, 9th Cir. 1974 [from-memory]).

name: Menominee Termination Act
citation: Act of June 17, 1954, ch. 303, 68 Stat. 250 (Pub. L. 83-399); effective Apr. 30, 1961
summary: Ended federal recognition of the Menominee; hunting and fishing rights survived under Menominee v. United States (1968). Reversed by the Menominee Restoration Act (1973).

name: Indian Relocation Act (Adult Vocational Training Act)
summary: Authorized a federal vocational training program for adult Indians living on or near reservations, with transportation to the place of training; the National Archives places it within the termination-era urban relocation program, which began earlier under other authority.

name: National Historic Preservation Act (Section 106; 1992 TCP amendments)
summary: Requires federal agencies to consider effects on historic properties, including properties of traditional religious and cultural importance to tribes, with tribal consultation (1992 amendments). Procedural protection for sacred sites.

name: Indian Civil Rights Act
summary: Applied many Bill of Rights protections to tribal governments (not the Establishment Clause or civil jury), capped tribal criminal punishment (originally six months/$500; raised to one year/$5,000 in 1986 and later expanded in 2010), required tribal consent for new state assumption of jurisdiction under PL 280, and provided habeas review.

name: Blue Lake Return Act (Taos Pueblo)
summary: Returned about 48,000 acres of mountain land, including Blue Lake, from the Carson National Forest to Taos Pueblo in trust, a landmark restoration of a sacred area.

name: Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA)
summary: Extinguished aboriginal title in Alaska in exchange for about 44 million acres and $962.5 million, delivered through regional and village corporations rather than reservations; Venetie (1998) held ANCSA lands are not Indian country.

name: Menominee Restoration Act
summary: Restored federal recognition of the Menominee Tribe, the first major reversal of termination.

name: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA)
citation: Pub. L. 93-638, signed Jan. 4, 1975; 25 U.S.C. 5301 et seq. (formerly 450); 88 Stat. 2203
summary: Authorized tribes to contract with and compact for federal programs, shifting program control to tribal governments; central to Becerra (2024) and Chehalis (2021).

name: American Indian Religious Freedom Act (AIRFA)
summary: Declared a federal policy to protect Native religious freedom, including access to sites; held in Lyng (1988) to create no judicially enforceable rights. Amended 1994 (Pub. L. 103-344) to protect sacramental peyote use.

name: Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA)
summary: Set federal standards for removal and adoption of Native children, tribal court jurisdiction, and placement preferences; upheld in Haaland v. Brackeen (2023).

name: Rhode Island Indian Claims Settlement Act
summary: Settled the Narragansett land claim for about 1,800 acres of land held in a state-chartered settlement corporation, the land at issue in Carcieri v. Salazar (2009).

name: Archaeological Resources Protection Act (ARPA)
summary: Protects archaeological resources on public and Indian lands and requires tribal consent or notice for excavation on Indian lands.

name: Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA)
summary: Established more than 100 million additional acres of federal conservation land in Alaska; Title VIII gives a rural (not Native-specific) subsistence priority, a source of ongoing Alaska Native subsistence conflict.

name: Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act (MICSA)
summary: Extinguished Maine tribes' aboriginal land claims in exchange for about $81.5 million, partly for acquiring up to 300,000 acres; subjected the tribes to Maine law and has been read to exclude them from some later federal Indian statutes.

name: Indian Land Consolidation Act (ILCA)
summary: Sought to reduce fractionated allotment ownership through escheat and consolidation; the escheat provision was struck down twice (Hodel v. Irving, 1987; Babbitt v. Youpee, 1997) and replaced by AIPRA (2004).

name: Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA)
summary: Created a framework for tribal gaming on 'Indian lands' with state-tribal compacts for casino-style gaming; ties economic development to the trust-land and Indian-lands definitions litigated in Carcieri-related and Bay Mills cases.

name: Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA)
citation: Pub. L. 101-601, 104 Stat. 3048 (Nov. 16, 1990); 25 U.S.C. 3001 et seq.; regulations at 43 C.F.R. part 10
summary: Requires federal agencies and federally funded museums to inventory and repatriate Native human remains, funerary and sacred objects, and objects of cultural patrimony; gives tribes ownership of cultural items on federal and tribal land.

name: Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act
summary: Settled the Catawba land claim (after South Carolina v. Catawba, 1986) for $50 million from federal, state, local and private parties ($32 million federal share) and authority to expand the reservation; restored the federal trust relationship.

name: American Indian Probate Reform Act (AIPRA)
summary: Overhauled intestate succession of trust and restricted allotments to curb fractionation; the 25 U.S.C. 2201 notes confirm the Act and an October 27, 2004 effective-date reference.

name: Claims Resolution Act of 2010 (Cobell settlement; Land Buy-Back Program)
summary: Funded the $3.4 billion Cobell settlement, including a $1.9 billion Land Consolidation Fund for the Land Buy-Back Program, which bought fractionated trust interests and returned them to tribal ownership (Interior reports it consolidated more than 800,000 interests, equivalent to 2.3 million acres; its 10-year period ended November 24, 2022).

name: Tribal Law and Order Act (TLOA)
citation: Pub. L. 111-211, 124 Stat. 2258 (July 29, 2010), tit. II (Tribal Law and Order Act of 2010) at 124 Stat. 2261
summary: Strengthened tribal sentencing authority (to 3 years), federal accountability and coordination in Indian country law enforcement.

name: Helping Expedite and Advance Responsible Tribal Homeownership (HEARTH) Act of 2012
summary: Lets tribes with Secretary-approved leasing regulations approve surface leases of tribal trust land (business and agricultural up to 25 years with renewals; certain others up to 75 years) without case-by-case Secretarial approval.

name: Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013 (tribal provisions)
summary: Recognized tribes' inherent power to prosecute non-Indians for domestic and dating violence and protection-order violations against Indian victims, partly overriding Oliphant (1978). Implemented in phases from 2013-2015 [phase dates from-memory].

name: Bears Ears National Monument Proclamation (Obama)
summary: Designated Bears Ears (about 1.36 million acres per 2026 sources) on a proposal by the Hopi, Navajo, Ute Mountain Ute, Ute Indian Tribe and Zuni; created the Bears Ears Commission.

name: Bears Ears reductions and restoration (2017 and 2021)
summary: The 2017 proclamation cut Bears Ears by roughly 83-87 percent depending on source (KUER: 83 percent; the Coalition: about 87 percent); Biden restored the monument and Commission in October 2021 and a cooperative agreement followed in summer 2022.

name: Violence Against Women Act Reauthorization of 2022 (tribal provisions)
citation: Pub. L. 117-103, div. W, tit. VIII, sec. 804 (Mar. 15, 2022), 136 Stat. 898 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022 begins at 136 Stat. 49); 25 U.S.C. 1304
summary: Expanded tribal jurisdiction over non-Indians to a broader list of covered crimes (including child violence, sexual violence, stalking, sex trafficking, assault of tribal justice personnel, obstruction of justice) and authorized $25 million per year for fiscal years 2023-2027. Alaska pilot [from-memory].

name: Land Acquisitions rule (25 C.F.R. part 151, fee-to-trust)
summary: Revised Interior's land-into-trust regulations to simplify and speed fee-to-trust acquisitions after listening and consultation sessions; status under the 2025-2026 administration not verified.

name: NAGPRA regulations (43 C.F.R. part 10), 2023 revision
summary: Revised systematic processes for disposition and repatriation, requiring museums and agencies to defer to Native American traditional knowledge of lineal descendants, tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations.

name: Lumbee Tribe federal recognition (NDAA enactment)
citation: Included in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Pub. L. 119-60 (S. 1071), signed Dec. 18, 2025 (Lumbee provision is section 8803 per the BIA list notice, 91 FR 4102); 139 Stat. 718
summary: Extended full federal recognition to the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina, ending the limbo created by the 1956 Lumbee Act, opening access to trust land, services and NAGPRA.

name: Solicitor's Opinion M-37087 (Alaska fee-to-trust)
citation: Solicitor William Doffermyre, M-37087 (Feb. 24, 2026), reversing M-37076 (Nov. 16, 2022)
summary: Withdrew the 2022 Solicitor opinion (M-37076) that found authority to take land in Alaska into trust under the IRA, and reinstated the 2021 opinion (M-37064) that found the earlier analysis insufficient; new Alaska applications to be rejected; Interior signaled a rulemaking that could affect lower-48 land acquisition rules.

name: Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante Proclamations (Trump)
citation: Proclamation 11043 (Bears Ears; 91 FR 45169) and Proclamation 11044 (Grand Staircase-Escalante; 91 FR 45179), signed July 13, 2026, published July 17, 2026
summary: Reduced Bears Ears from about 1.36 million acres to 121,096 acres (about 91 percent) and Grand Staircase-Escalante from about 1.87 million to 181,541 acres; disbanded the Bears Ears Commission; excluded about 1,238,904 acres, which the proclamation opens to entry, mineral leasing and mining location, subject to valid existing rights.

name: Apology Resolution (Pub. L. 103-150)
summary: Joint resolution acknowledging the 100th anniversary of the January 17, 1893 overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawai'i and apologizing to Native Hawaiians on behalf of the United States; it states that the Native Hawaiian people never directly relinquished their claims to sovereignty over their national lands. It settles no claims.
